study.title: Praise the name of the LORD
study.intro: Psalm 135 is a hymn of praise that gathers phrases from across the Old Testament into one great call to worship. It praises the LORD for choosing Israel, for ruling over all creation, for rescuing His people from Egypt and giving them a land. Then it mocks the lifeless idols of the nations and calls every group in Israel to bless the God who actually lives and acts.
study.context: Psalm 135 follows Psalm 134's call to the temple servants and expands it. Much of it echoes other Scripture: Exodus, Deuteronomy, Jeremiah 10:13 and Psalm 115:4-11, which it nearly quotes about idols. It recounts the plagues on Egypt and the defeat of the kings Sihon and Og east of the Jordan (Numbers 21:21-35). It pairs naturally with Psalm 136, which retells the same story as a responsive litany.
study.peopleNote: No author is named. Israel is called Jacob, God's treasured possession. Pharaoh, Sihon and Og appear as defeated rulers. The houses of Aaron and Levi are the priests and temple servants. God is never portrayed as a human figure in planned art.

verses.title: A call to praise
verses.heading: Give praise, O servants of the LORD
verses.meaning: 'Hallelujah! Praise the name of the LORD. Give praise, O servants of the LORD,' The psalm bursts open with 'Hallelujah,' which means 'praise the LORD.' It calls God's servants to honor His name, His character and reputation. Praise is not a mood we wait to feel; it is a calling. Those who belong to God and serve Him are first of all invited to celebrate who He is.
verses.context: Psalm 134:1 called the servants of the LORD to bless Him by night. Psalm 113:1 opens with almost the same words. Hebrews 13:15 urges believers to offer a continual sacrifice of praise to God.
explore: Hallelujah
A Hebrew call meaning 'praise the LORD,' from hallelu (praise) and Yah (the LORD).
Name of the LORD
God's revealed character and reputation, everything He has shown Himself to be.
verses.reflect: What about God's character can you praise Him for today?
verses.alt: Temple courtyard at morning with worshipers gathering on the steps.

verses.title: Standing in His courts
verses.heading: In the courts of the house of our God
verses.meaning: 'who stand in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God.' The call is aimed at those who serve and worship in the temple. To stand there is a privilege: being in the place of God's presence, in the courts where His people gather. Those closest to God's house have the most reason to praise, and today every believer has been brought near.
verses.context: The temple had courts where priests served and where Israelites gathered to worship. Psalm 84:2 longs for the courts of the LORD. Ephesians 2:13 says those once far away have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
explore: Courts
Open courtyards around the temple where priests served and worshipers gathered to pray.
Stand
To serve or attend, ready to act; standing was the posture of priests on duty.
verses.reflect: How does it feel to know you have been brought near to God's presence?
verses.alt: Priests in plain linen standing in a sunlit stone courtyard.

verses.title: Praise for a good God
verses.heading: For the LORD is good
verses.meaning: 'Hallelujah, for the LORD is good; sing praises to His name, for it is lovely.' Here is the first reason to praise: God is good. He is not cruel, distant or unpredictable but kind and right in everything. And praising Him is lovely, pleasant and fitting. Singing about a good God is one of the most delightful things a person can do. Worship is not a burden but a joy.
verses.context: Psalm 147:1 says it is good to sing praises to our God, for it is pleasant and praise is fitting. Psalm 34:8 invites us to taste and see that the LORD is good. Nahum 1:7 says the LORD is good, a refuge in trouble.
explore: Good
Morally excellent and kind; God's goodness is the source of every good thing.
Lovely
Pleasant and delightful; the Hebrew can describe both God's name and the act of praising it.
verses.reflect: When was the last time praising God felt delightful to you? What made it so?
verses.alt: Musicians with lyres and drums playing under a fig tree.

verses.title: A treasured possession
verses.heading: Israel as His treasured possession
verses.meaning: 'For the LORD has chosen Jacob as His own, Israel as His treasured possession.' Here is a second reason to praise: God chose His people. Out of all nations He took Israel as His own special treasure, like a king's personal jewels. This choice was not earned; it came from His love. The New Testament says that in Christ believers too are God's treasured people.
verses.context: Exodus 19:5 says Israel would be God's treasured possession among all peoples. Deuteronomy 7:7-8 says God chose Israel not because they were many but because He loved them. 1 Peter 2:9 calls believers a people for God's own possession.
explore: Treasured possession
A special personal treasure, like the private jewels of a king.
Chosen
Selected by God's free decision and love, not because of the people's merit.
verses.reflect: How does it change you to know God treasures you as His own?
verses.alt: A small wooden chest of polished stones and jewels in lamplight.

verses.title: Above all gods
verses.heading: Our Lord is above all gods
verses.meaning: 'For I know that the LORD is great; our Lord is above all gods.' The psalmist speaks personally: 'I know.' This is not a guess but a conviction. The LORD is great, greater than every so-called god the nations worshiped. Whatever people bow down to, money, power, success or idols, none can compare with Him. Knowing His greatness gives confidence and frees us from serving lesser things.
verses.context: Exodus 18:11 records Jethro saying, 'Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods.' Psalm 95:3 calls the LORD a great King above all gods. 1 Corinthians 8:5-6 says there is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ.
explore: Great
Mighty, majestic and beyond comparison in power and worth.
Gods
The false gods of the nations, idols and powers people worshiped instead of the LORD.
verses.reflect: What 'gods' compete for your trust? How does God's greatness put them in their place?
verses.alt: Broken clay figurines lying in the dust at the foot of a hill.

verses.title: He does what pleases Him
verses.heading: In the seas and in all their depths
verses.meaning: 'The LORD does all that pleases Him in the heavens and on the earth, in the seas and in all their depths.' God is free and sovereign. Every part of creation, from the sky to the deepest ocean, is under His rule. Nothing is outside His reach. This is a comfort: the same God who rules everywhere is good and has chosen His people. His freedom is not random; it is the freedom of perfect love.
verses.context: Psalm 115:3 says our God is in heaven and does as He pleases. Daniel 4:35 says no one can hold back His hand. Ephesians 1:11 says He works all things according to the counsel of His will.
explore: Pleases Him
What God desires and chooses, always in line with His good and wise character.
Depths
The deepest parts of the sea, places beyond human reach that God still rules.
verses.reflect: What part of your life do you need to trust is under God's good rule?
verses.alt: Waves rolling across a wide sea under a towering sky of clouds.

verses.title: Lord of the storm
verses.heading: Brings forth the wind from His storehouses
verses.meaning: 'He causes the clouds to rise from the ends of the earth. He generates the lightning with the rain and brings forth the wind from His storehouses.' Weather is not run by storm gods, as Israel's neighbors believed. The LORD lifts the clouds, sends lightning with rain and releases the wind as if from storehouses. Every storm and every rain shower is under His command.
verses.context: Canaanites worshiped Baal as god of storms and rain. Jeremiah 10:13 uses nearly the same words for the LORD. Elijah showed the LORD alone sends rain (1 Kings 18:41-45). Job 38:22 speaks of the storehouses of snow and hail.
explore: Storehouses
Places where supplies are kept; a poetic picture of God's reserves of wind and weather.
Lightning
Flashes of light in a storm, seen in Scripture as a display of God's power.
verses.reflect: The next time you see a storm, how could it remind you of God's power?
verses.alt: Storm clouds rising over distant hills with rain and a flash of lightning.

verses.title: The firstborn of Egypt
verses.heading: Of both man and beast
verses.meaning: 'He struck down the firstborn of Egypt, of both man and beast.' The psalm turns from creation to history. The final plague in Egypt broke Pharaoh's grip on Israel. It was a solemn judgment on a nation that had enslaved and killed Israel's sons. God showed He alone is Lord over life and death, and that He would keep His promise to free His people.
verses.context: Exodus 12:29 tells of the death of Egypt's firstborn at midnight. Israel was spared through the Passover lamb's blood (Exodus 12:13), which the New Testament connects to Christ our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).
explore: Firstborn
The oldest son, who held special honor and inheritance rights in ancient families.
Passover
The night God passed over Israelite homes marked by lamb's blood, sparing their firstborn.
verses.reflect: How does the Passover help you understand what Jesus did for you?
verses.alt: Doorframes marked with red at night in a quiet village street.

verses.title: Signs and wonders
verses.heading: Against Pharaoh and all his servants
verses.meaning: 'He sent signs and wonders into your midst, O Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants.' The psalm suddenly addresses Egypt directly, as if speaking to the nation. The plagues were signs and wonders, miracles that pointed to the true God and exposed Egypt's gods as powerless. Pharaoh and his officials thought they were in control, but God showed otherwise.
verses.context: Exodus 7:3 says God would multiply signs and wonders in Egypt. Exodus 12:12 says God would execute judgment on all the gods of Egypt. Deuteronomy 4:34 asks if any god ever took a nation for himself by signs and wonders.
explore: Signs
Miracles that point beyond themselves to show who God is and what He is doing.
Wonders
Astonishing acts that cause awe because they go beyond the ordinary.
verses.reflect: What 'signs' of God's work have you noticed in your own life?
verses.alt: A palace courtyard in Egypt under a darkened, swarming sky.

verses.title: Mighty kings struck down
verses.heading: He struck down many nations
verses.meaning: 'He struck down many nations and slaughtered mighty kings:' After the exodus, Israel faced powerful kings on the way to the promised land. They could not have defeated them alone. God fought for them. These victories are remembered not to glorify war but to show God's faithfulness in keeping His promise to give His people a home, no matter who stood in the way.
verses.context: Numbers 21 recounts victories east of the Jordan, and Joshua 12 lists the kings defeated in Canaan. Deuteronomy 7:1 says God would drive out nations greater and stronger than Israel. Romans 8:31 asks who can be against us if God is for us.
explore: Nations
Peoples who lived in or near Canaan and opposed Israel on the way to the promised land.
Mighty kings
Powerful rulers with strong armies who seemed unbeatable by human strength.
verses.reflect: What 'mighty' obstacle stands between you and what God has called you to?
verses.alt: Fortified hilltop towns seen across a wide plain at evening.

verses.title: Sihon and Og
verses.heading: Sihon king of the Amorites, Og king of Bashan
verses.meaning: 'Sihon king of the Amorites, Og king of Bashan, and all the kings of Canaan.' The psalm names names. Sihon and Og were the first great kings Israel defeated east of the Jordan, and their defeat became a famous memory of God's faithfulness. Og was remembered as a giant. Naming them makes the story concrete. God's help is not vague; it shows up in real places and real victories.
verses.context: Numbers 21:21-35 tells of the defeat of Sihon and Og. Deuteronomy 3:11 describes Og's huge iron bed. Joshua 2:10 shows Rahab in Jericho had heard what God did to Sihon and Og.
explore: Amorites
A Canaanite people; Sihon ruled an Amorite kingdom east of the Jordan River.
Bashan
A fertile region northeast of the Sea of Galilee, ruled by the giant king Og.
verses.reflect: What specific victories can you name where God came through for you?
verses.alt: Rolling green pastures of Bashan with basalt stone ruins.

verses.title: Land as inheritance
verses.heading: As a heritage to His people Israel
verses.meaning: 'He gave their land as an inheritance, as a heritage to His people Israel.' The victories had a purpose: a home. God gave the land to Israel as an inheritance, a gift passed down from a father to his children. They did not earn it; they received it. Everything God's people have is ultimately a gift from His hand, given to be cared for and passed on.
verses.context: God promised Abraham the land in Genesis 15:18. Joshua 21:43 says the LORD gave Israel all the land He swore to give their fathers. 1 Peter 1:4 speaks of an inheritance that can never perish, kept in heaven for believers.
explore: Inheritance
Property passed down to heirs, received as a gift rather than earned.
Heritage
Something valuable handed down and belonging to a family over generations.
verses.reflect: What has God given you as an inheritance that you want to care for and pass on?
verses.alt: Terraced fields and vineyards spreading across sunny hills.

verses.title: A name that endures
verses.heading: Your renown through all generations
verses.meaning: 'Your name, O LORD, endures forever, Your renown, O LORD, through all generations.' Kings like Sihon and Og are long gone, but God's name lasts forever. His fame does not fade with time. Every generation hears again what He has done. Human reputations rise and fall, but God's renown keeps growing as each new generation learns to trust Him.
verses.context: Exodus 3:15 says the LORD's name is His name forever, remembered from generation to generation. Psalm 102:12 says His renown endures through all generations. Philippians 2:9-11 says every knee will bow at the name of Jesus.
explore: Renown
Fame and honor, the memory of someone's great deeds spread widely.
Generations
Each new group of people born in a family or nation, one after another.
verses.reflect: How are you helping the next generation hear about God's name?
verses.alt: An old man telling a story to children gathered around a fire.

verses.title: Vindicated and comforted
verses.heading: Compassion on His servants
verses.meaning: 'For the LORD will vindicate His people and will have compassion on His servants.' God will defend His people and show them mercy. To vindicate is to set right and clear someone's name. Even when God's people suffer or fail, He does not abandon them. This line is quoted from Moses' song in Deuteronomy, a promise that God's compassion outlasts every hard season.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 32:36 says the LORD will vindicate His people and have compassion on His servants. Hebrews 10:30 quotes this same line. Psalm 103:13 says as a father has compassion on his children, so the LORD on those who fear Him.
explore: Vindicate
To defend, judge in favor of, and clear someone's name before others.
Compassion
Deep pity and tender care for someone in pain or need.
verses.reflect: Where do you need God to vindicate you or show compassion to you right now?
verses.alt: A mother lifting a fallen child from the ground in a village lane.

verses.title: Silver and gold idols
verses.heading: Made by the hands of men
verses.meaning: 'The idols of the nations are silver and gold, made by the hands of men.' Now the psalm contrasts the living God with idols. They may be made of precious metals and look impressive, but they are crafted by human hands. A god you make yourself cannot be greater than you. Every idol, ancient or modern, is ultimately something people make and then mistakenly trust.
verses.context: Verses 15-18 echo Psalm 115:4-8 almost word for word. Isaiah 44:9-20 mocks a carpenter who makes an idol from half a log and burns the other half. Acts 17:29 says the divine is not like gold or silver formed by human skill.
explore: Idols
Images or objects worshiped as gods; anything trusted in place of the true God.
Hands of men
Human craftsmanship, things people design and build themselves.
verses.reflect: What things made by human hands are you tempted to trust more than God?
verses.alt: A craftsman's bench with a half-finished metal figure and tools.

verses.title: Mouths that cannot speak
verses.heading: Eyes, but cannot see
verses.meaning: 'They have mouths, but cannot speak; they have eyes, but cannot see;' The idols have faces but no life. Their mouths never answer prayer and their eyes never see people's needs. In contrast, the LORD speaks His word and sees His people's suffering. The irony is sharp: people pray to things that cannot hear them, while the God who sees and speaks is ignored.
verses.context: Jeremiah 10:5 says idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field that cannot speak. Exodus 3:7 says God has seen the misery of His people. Habakkuk 2:18 asks what profit an idol is that its maker trusts in it.
explore: Mouths
Openings for speech; an idol's carved mouth looks real but can never answer.
Irony
A situation where things turn out the opposite of what is expected, often exposing foolishness.
verses.reflect: How does it comfort you that God sees and speaks, unlike any idol?
verses.alt: A carved stone face with blank eyes covered in moss.

verses.title: No breath in them
verses.heading: Nor is there breath in their mouths
verses.meaning: 'they have ears, but cannot hear; nor is there breath in their mouths.' The idols cannot hear a single prayer, and they have no breath, no life at all. The living God breathed life into humanity at creation. Idols cannot even breathe themselves. Trusting them is like asking a statue for help. Only the God who gives breath can give life and answer those who call.
verses.context: Genesis 2:7 says God breathed into man the breath of life. Jeremiah 10:14 says idols have no breath in them. Acts 17:25 says God Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.
explore: Breath
Air breathed in and out; in Scripture a sign of life given by God.
Ears
Organs of hearing; an idol's carved ears cannot hear even the loudest prayer.
verses.reflect: Who has God given breath to that you can thank Him for today?
verses.alt: A dusty clay statue standing silent in an abandoned shrine.

verses.title: Becoming like what we trust
verses.heading: Those who make them become like them
verses.meaning: 'Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them.' Here is a sobering truth: we become like what we worship. People who trust lifeless idols become spiritually lifeless themselves, blind and deaf to God. But the reverse is also true: those who worship the living God are being made more like Him, alive and responsive to His voice.
verses.context: Psalm 115:8 says the same. 2 Kings 17:15 says Israel followed worthless idols and became worthless. 2 Corinthians 3:18 says believers, beholding the Lord's glory, are being transformed into His image.
explore: Trust
To rely on and put confidence in someone or something for help and security.
Become like
To be shaped over time into the character of what one admires and worships.
verses.reflect: What are you becoming like because of what you give your attention and trust to?
verses.alt: A worn statue and a living tree standing side by side in a courtyard.

verses.title: Israel and Aaron, bless
verses.heading: O house of Aaron, bless the LORD
verses.meaning: 'O house of Israel, bless the LORD; O house of Aaron, bless the LORD;' The psalm returns to praise, calling group by group. First the whole nation, then the priestly family of Aaron. Everyone has a part. In contrast to silent idols, God's people are meant to be loud with blessing for the living God. Praise is a community song, not a solo.
verses.context: Psalm 115:9-11 and 118:2-4 also call Israel, the house of Aaron and those who fear the LORD. Aaron was Israel's first high priest (Exodus 28:1). Colossians 3:16 urges singing to God with gratitude in your hearts.
explore: House of Israel
The whole nation of Israel, all the descendants of Jacob together.
House of Aaron
The priestly family descended from Aaron, Moses' brother and Israel's first high priest.
verses.reflect: How can you join with others in your community to bless the LORD this week?
verses.alt: A large crowd in a courtyard raising hands with priests on the steps.

verses.title: Levi and all who fear
verses.heading: You who fear the LORD, bless the LORD
verses.meaning: 'O house of Levi, bless the LORD; you who fear the LORD, bless the LORD!' The call widens. The Levites who served in the temple are added, and then everyone who fears the LORD, including people from other nations who had come to trust Israel's God. The circle of praise keeps growing. Anyone who honors God is invited to bless Him.
verses.context: The Levites assisted the priests and led temple music (1 Chronicles 23:28-30). 'Those who fear the LORD' may include Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God, like Cornelius in Acts 10:2. Revelation 19:5 calls all God's servants who fear Him to praise.
explore: Levi
The tribe set apart to serve in the tabernacle and temple, assisting the priests.
Fear the LORD
To honor God with reverent awe and trust, the posture of true worship.
verses.reflect: How does it encourage you that anyone who fears the LORD is invited to praise?
verses.alt: Levite singers with cymbals and harps on temple steps.

verses.title: Blessed from Zion
verses.heading: He who dwells in Jerusalem
verses.meaning: 'Blessed be the LORD from Zion—He who dwells in Jerusalem. Hallelujah!' The psalm closes where it began, with Hallelujah. God is blessed from Zion, the place where He chose to dwell among His people. Psalm 134 ended with God blessing His people from Zion; here His people bless Him back from Zion. Blessing flows both ways between God and those He loves.
verses.context: Psalm 134:3 had the LORD blessing His people from Zion. Psalm 76:2 says His dwelling place is in Zion. Revelation 21:3 promises God's dwelling with humanity forever.
explore: Dwells
Lives and makes His home; God chose to make His presence known in Jerusalem.
Blessed be
A phrase of praise, honoring God and declaring His goodness.
verses.reflect: How can you return blessing to God for the blessings He has given you?
verses.alt: Jerusalem's walls glowing at sunset with the temple on the hill.
